  We start by reviewing existing data stream classifiers and their underlying processing methods, before categorizing these classifiers into two groups: classical methods, including Nearest Neighbor, Decision Tree, and AdaBoost; and Deep Learning methods, including Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks. 

  From a cloud provider's standpoint, we analyze the advantages and limitations of both approaches, before presenting a practical example of using Boosting method to classify data streams from high-dimensional sources to low-dimensional ones. 

  Ultimately, our study suggests that the choice of data stream classifier should be guided by a balance between its accuracy and the resources required to support it. 

  We present our observations in this report, along with an accompanying video that demonstrates the cloud resources required to support these classifiers. 

  Similar to the video "How Google Chrome uses CPU/Memory", this video aims to illustrate the operational principles of data stream classifiers from the cloud provider's perspective, utilizing popular data streams from high-dimensional sources to low-dimensional ones for demonstration purposes, available at: https://youtu.be/FYs8PTJsyXA. 

  From a technical standpoint, our study complements previous research in classifying data stream classifiers from the perspective of applications, highlighting the differences in computational requirements, model complexities, and potential applications of both techniques. 

  Based on our investigation, our study reveals that Deep Learning methods generally demand more computational resources, longer training times, and greater storage capacity than classical methods. 

  Nonetheless, our results show that the superior accuracy of Deep Learning methods often justify the additional computational costs involved in processing the data. 

  For instance, Deep Learning methods for sentiment analysis on Netflix and Twitter, for example, have been shown to outperform other algorithms by a margin of up to 3%. 

  From the viewpoint of cloud users, our study indicates that the choice of classifier depends on the specific application - for instance, Boosting methods have been shown to provide near state-of-the-art performance across various platforms while saving significant computational resources.

  Our study further shows that both approaches have the potential to significantly reduce the energy consumption of data stream classifiers.

A straightforward approach involves measuring the bias experienced by each individual group, and then adjusting for the variability among these groups. Yet, several factors complicate this strategy: Firstly, many group identities are predetermined by factors such as a person's ethnicity or gender. Secondly, some group memberships are shaped by historical contexts, like the legacy of slavery in a particular region. Lastly, social bias can be transmitted from one generation to the next, leading to persistent group inequalities. 
 
 We propose a framework that addresses these complexities. Our approach recognizes that group affiliations can be either predetermined or derived from past historical events. Additionally, we develop a method that adjusts for the variability among these groups, by measuring the bias experienced by individual groups and using statistical correlations to remove the impact of unique characteristics within each group. This results in a more accurate adjustment of the bias experienced by all groups, rather than relying on partial measurements of this adjustment. 
 
 We demonstrate our results through two real-world examples. In our first study, we investigate racial bias in employment by examining a dataset that includes demographic information such as company location and employee status. Given the variability among different companies and the fact that racial group memberships are largely historical in nature, we show that our proposed method effectively adjusts for these factors to measure the overall bias experienced by individual racial groups. 
 
 In our second study, we aim to identify the extent to which a particular social bias affects one group over another. We apply our method to a scenario in which a social bias affects some groups based on characteristics like income and education, but the direct impact of this bias varies from one group to another. 
 
 Both studies show that our proposed framework delivers more effective bias measurements that reveal nuanced relationships between different group identities and social bias. Moreover, these measurements serve as valuable indicators in addressing social bias. To automate the process of conducting bias analysis, we provide a comprehensive, open-source analysis tool that includes our proposed framework as a key feature. This tool analyzes social bias based on group affiliations and allows users to derive a comprehensive analysis of this bias from a feature called Racial Bias Explorer. Users can access this tool through https://github.com/LDA-Centre/RacialBiasExplorer. 
 
 We discuss the implications of our research, which we hope will pave the way for further investigations in the field of performing bias analysis. Extensive results from our research can be found at http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5189533.

To reduce the computational demands of encoders within these models, two approaches - factorized time-frequency space and cross-frame factorized space - were tested and compared. By applying these methods to the T-F space of mel-frequency ceppl (60) features, the models' time-frame interaction complexity was significantly reduced, with minimal impact on recognition accuracy. For example, when using the factorized time-frequency space, the model's computational complexity was reduced from 689B to 384B multiplications, a 57% decrease. Similarly, the cross-frame factorized space method significantly decreased the model's acoustic feature computation complexity by a factor of 65 compared to the traditional implementation. These simplified models were then applied to the CSJ corpus, yielding significant gains in recognition accuracy over the standard, non-factorized model. Notably, when using the factorized time-frequency space, the model's performance increased by 0.3% to reach 88.3% accuracy, and when using the cross-frame factorized space, the model's performance increased by 0.6% to reach 88.5% accuracy. Additionally, the factorized time-frequency space approach yielded consistent, albeit minor, decreases in recognition accuracy when used on the Timit and Switchboard speech databases, but resulted in modest performance improvements of 0.8% and 0.6%, respectively. Finally, the cross-frame factorized space approach was tested on the Timit and Switchboard speech databases, yielding recognition accuracy improvements of 0.8% and 0.6%, respectively, highlighting the model's increased interpretability and aiding word error rate reductions due to the factorized space. These simplified models also led to the discovery of the significance of encoder acoustic feature computation complexity in model recognition accuracy through linear regression analysis. Overall, the heavily factorized models developed in this study demonstrate the potential for substantial accuracy improvements and still achieve very competitive recognition accuracy. These models also remain relatively intuitive due to the retention of traditional feature extraction methods. Nonetheless, the heavily factorized models still surpass traditional models in understanding the interaction between the encoder and the decoding process, allowing for the incorporation of factorized spaces in other areas, such as the encoder decoding interaction. We focus on systems with piecewise constant excitation and discrete-valued measurements. Our results rely on theoretical validation, leveraging properties of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and their associated norms, particularly the trace norm. We demonstrate the convergence of one-step and N-step estimators and compare their respective convergence rates, which are influenced by the characteristics of the system, its piecewise excitations, and measurements. Our findings show that, under comparable conditions, one-step estimators exhibit faster convergence than N-step estimators. Additionally, we show that converging estimators maintain their convergence rate as the number of data points increases, which is not observed in converging but divergent estimators. Our approach leverages the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Jacobian to generate an empirical graph that accurately represents the implicit functions representing the network's layers. We establish that the eigenvalues are non-negative and that the correlation between adjacent nodes in the graph and the eigenvector-related properties justify the application of a graph-based model. We further introduce computational graph metrics that enable us to investigate various training dynamics, for example: We employ graph analysis to predict the occurrence of gradient vanishing or exploding during stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We utilize graph analysis to identify the presence of local minima and determine that deeper networks tend to have more topological structures. We introduce a graph analysis to establish that Label Leakage occurs through the edges that connect input and output nodes. We develop an analysis based on the computational graph that confirms that stochastic gradient descent can be viewed as a diffusion process. Our study marks the first attempt to establish a geometric framework for neural networks during training, in addition to uncovering insights that illuminate the mechanistic understandability of neural networks, which can also foster the development of more refined algorithms and networks. For instance: We propose an edge-weighted algorithm that expands upon plateau-tackling strategies, selecting nodes with high influence; We introduce Depth-aware Pruning, a method that offers a versatile framework for tuning graph structural parameters, preserving geometric invariants to ensure invariance; We develop a method that decouples diffusion dynamics from the learning process to ensure robustness and adoptability. This whole slide evaluation approach offers reduced data storage, accelerated review times, and enhanced reviewer consistency.  However, there is a need for parameter optimization when training CNNs on WSIs due to the variation in data quality, resulting from factors such as staining, imaging, and sliding. Specifically, we investigate how interaction affects the conductance through a double cone in two different scenarios: one where the Fermi level is within the bulk conduction band and another where it's at the band edge after hybridization with the contact leads. In the first scenario, a phase transition from a blockaded to a ballistic state can be induced by increasing the tunneling strength with the leads. In the second scenario, strong coupling to the leads causes the band edge to become fully delocalized, resulting in a ballistic state. Moreover, we explore the current versus voltage characteristic for both cases and observe that charge is not evenly distributed among the two cones under certain conditions, despite both exhibiting ballistic behavior. This non-uniform charge distribution impacts the chemical potential and influences the conductance, revealing that the conductance is not solely determined by the phase relaxation rate but also by the quasiparticle relaxation rate. Our analysis also reveals that Coulomb coupling between the two cones is essential to achieving a ballistic state. Multiple techniques have been proposed to address this issue, including model-based and model-agnostic methods that employ tabu, random-chassis, and CHC algorithms. These methods iteratively eliminate unsuitable search space sub-components to reduce exploration time. Although these approaches can lower costs in large search spaces, they struggle with high costs in real-world NAS deployments where the search space is often small. In contrast, we present NAS-tb, a novel approach that reformulates NAS into a tabu problem suited to parallel processing via affinity binding. NAS-tb is seamlessly integrated into popular deep learning frameworks, enabling it to efficiently handle small search spaces and meet the high-iteration demands of NAS deployments. Experimentation across widely used datasets demonstrates NAS-tb's cost reduction capabilities, with affinitization yielding improved generalization at equivalent costs, and also producing models that are structurally distinct from those generated by model-based and model-agnostic methods. Furthermore, we showcase the potential of deployment cost savings with NAS-tb, coupled with a novel transfer learning technique, achieving an 8-fold reduction in deployment costs on multiple datasets. In this paper, we introduce the concept of learning algorithms being improved using analyzed results, presenting an innovative technique for modifying a classifier's output based on predictive diagnostics from the tested inputs. The improvement is achieved through an energy-minimizing approach, drawing from the principles of thermodynamics and a well-established framework for dealing with internal states in statistical physics originally developed by Derrida and others. Predictive diagnostics for this purpose typically come in three forms: evaluation metrics, anomaly detection tests, and predictive sensitivity analysis tools. Each of these methods will be explained, reviewed, and discussed in more detail, along with concrete practical applications demonstrated using datasets from various fields. Moreover, a unique case study illustrates the value of collaborative machine learning and data learning, where insights from analyzed results guide the modification of an algorithm's output to yield better practical results, ultimately leading to the development of a new generic class of diagnostic-re-optimizable learning algorithms. These algorithms, in turn, facilitate the establishment of direct feedback loops between analyzed data, commonly referred to as "learning from data without a model," as well as the creation of adaptive probabilistic ensemble methods, balancing accuracy and robustness in decision-making processes. Consequently, the approach described here has far-reaching implications for dealiased machine learning, where analyzed results can be used to improve both single algorithms and complex networks of decision-making processes in various applications. The growing number of experimental data provides valuable information to improve our understanding.  Despite significant research, predicting protein-DNA interactions remains a significant challenge.  The aim of this study is to propose a novel method, called PDI_SALSA, for identifying potential interaction sites on DNA with given protein sequences.  To this end, a neural network model is trained using a large set of saliency features derived from both proteins and DNA, utilizing the ULTRA protocol to extract ULTRA-based DNA properties. To assess the performance of the proposed method, a five-fold cross-validation test on a substantial dataset of 1045 protein-DNA pairs was conducted, demonstrating improved performance over current leading methods.  The proposed method achieves a mean average precision of 0.456 across all DNA sequences, with significant improvement over the leading method, CASP12-DSPR.  To further verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, a non-systematic test on a second, independent dataset was conducted, resulting in even better performance with a mean average precision of 0.480.  Given the substantial training dataset and the unrelated nature of the tested pairs, this outcome confirms the potential of the proposed method to make a significant contribution to the prediction of protein-DNA interaction sites on DNA sequences. A question posed by Galashov and Xiang seeks a determination of graphs whose underlying symmetric double graphs exhibit perfect matching. In this study, we identify the specified graphs whose symmetric doubles yield perfect matching graphs, and demonstrate that such graphs must either be complete or contain no more than three vertices. Furthermore, we establish that every complete graph and every graph consisting of three connected components with at most two edges in each is a candidate for a graph whose symmetric double exhibits a perfect matching. By contrast, we prove that no graph comprising at least four connected components with at most two edges in each possesses this property. In addition to our findings, we prove that any graph whose symmetric double displays a perfect matching must either be a complete graph or have three vertices, and that the vertex set of such a graph may be partitioned into at most four independent sets. Finally, we prove that any sequence of complete graphs whose symmetric doubles exhibit perfect matchings must converge to either the complete graph on three vertices or the complete graph on four vertices. An examination is also conducted into the existence of graphs whose symmetric doubles display a Hamiltonian path; however, the sought-after class of graphs could not be determined. Finally, we prove that any graph whose symmetric double displays a Hamiltonian path must either be a complete graph or have three vertices, and that the vertex set of such a graph may be partitioned into at most four independent paths. In addition to our findings, we prove that any sequence of complete graphs whose symmetric doubles display Hamiltonian paths must converge to either the complete graph on three vertices or the complete graph on four vertices. Researchers have made headway in pinpointing specific social values such as cooperation, fairness, and trust, but there is still much to be explored in understanding these values and how they interact with each other. Meanwhile, a growing body of literature treats a functioning society as a whole and seeks to quantify its overall well-being, albeit without delving into the intricacies of its component parts. Our work aims to bridge this gap by developing a framework to track changes in social values at a large scale, and evaluating it using real-world data from online communities consisting of human participants. Our results demonstrate that our approach is practical and functional, paving the way for its application in various settings, such as analyzing massive online groups or forecasting societal transitions. Additionally, this framework may also be adapted for analyzing interactions between a society and its surroundings. We propose a framework to improve the stability of these networks by training them to produce consistent outputs across different setups. The framework consists of three key components: 1) a method to measure variability in the networks' behavior; 2) a metric to evaluate the impact of changes on the overall performance; 3) an optimization technique to refine the networks to be resilient to such changes. We demonstrate this framework using various neural networks and datasets, and our results show its effectiveness and efficiency. The framework is available at https://github.com/megpy/pytorch-mean.git for replication purposes. Furthermore, our research also reveals that networks composed of different computational elements exhibit distinct patterns of variability. For instance, networks with spiking neural dynamics (such as SNNs) tend to produce more consistent results when the inputs have the same overall structure, whereas other networks are more affected by changes in individual input elements. This insight could be a crucial factor to consider when developing new types of neuromorphic networks. The framework we devised could be a valuable resource to develop future networks that are resistant to variability, including those based on spiking networks. In addition to its applications in neuromorphic computing, this framework could also be relevant to areas such as network neuroscience and neuroengineering, where modeling biological networks with uncertainty is inherent to the model. From an applications perspective, our research could also be relevant to experimental techniques in neuroscience such as intrinsic conditional sensitivity, which could be used to develop new experimental techniques to investigate brain circuits. , managing and coordinating networks has become increasingly complex. Notably, the increase in traffic and the diversity of traffic have exacerbated issues with congestion, delay, and unfairness. To tackle these challenges, various advanced networking technologies have been developed, such as Software Defined Networking (SDN), Cloud Radio Access Networking (CRAN), and network slicing. The potential of these technologies for future mobile networks and the next generation of wireless communication systems is significant. Nevertheless, the integration and efficient application of these technologies also pose difficulties and numerous open technical questions. In this paper, we explore the relationships, applications, and management approaches for SDN, CRAN, and network slicing. Firstly, we explain their characteristics and benefits, and then outline their roles in the next generation of wireless communication systems. Furthermore, we discuss the requirements for implementing these technologies and highlight the obstacles associated with their integration. Finally, we present innovative research opportunities in this area. The paper also provides a practical scenario illustrating how SDN and network slicing can collaborate to enhance the performance of wireless edge computing networks for ultra-reliable low-latency communications. The results show that network slicing offers greater flexibility than traditional network structures, which can lead to improved traffic demands and more efficient network operations when combined with SDN. Moreover, the number of required networks scales with the number of user demands, which can be significantly reduced when network slicing is used in conjunction with SDN. This research demonstrates the potential of network slicing to meet the requirements of wireless edge computing networks, which can help to meet the ultra-reliable low-latency communication needs of diverse services, such as those requiring latency below 1 ms and high data rates of 1 Gbit/s or higher. The integration of network slicing and SDN facilitates the efficient management of networks, which can contribute significantly to the development of next-generation wireless communication systems. The integration of network slicing and SDN offers the potential for network adaptability to be utilized fully in 6G, which may lead to an increase in service creativity, user engagement, and revenue, which can ultimately drive innovation in the telecommunications industry, leading to significant economic growth. The potential of network slicing and SDN to contribute significantly to the development of 6G has also sparked new questions regarding advanced wireless system functionalities and the management of wireless networks, which are discussed in this paper. To tackle these challenges, the paper explores advanced use cases and introduces novel concepts, such as the topological network slicing technique, which leverages virtualization to support diverse services over a shared wireless network infrastructure. To determine optimal generation plans, probabilistic forecasts can be utilized in stochastic gradient descent to identify an operational strategy that minimizes expected costs. Notably, this method assumes each node can access load forecasts from all its connections. If node-level forecasts are available, a centralized approach can combine them to determine an efficient operation strategy, but this requires coordinating with all nodes, which is impractical. A novel, decentralized algorithm is proposed to enable nodes to devise independent operation plans using their private generation costs and load forecasts, without necessitating coordination or shared load forecasts. It is proven that nodes can still minimize expected costs and constraints under uncertain load conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that nodes can achieve cost reductions of up to 9% compared to sequential LASSO methods. When applying this algorithm to networks with multiple nodes, a 4% cost improvement is observed for all nodes, despite using initial forecasts that are inaccurate. Furthermore, a 6% cost improvement can be achieved when incorporating social learning, yielding a total network cost reduction of 20%. These outcomes highlight the potential for substantial operational cost savings through LASSO-based social learning in complex distribution networks. As an extension of this work, exploring the scalability of social learning in actual networks, along with investigating other optimization objectives, remains a topic for future study. To facilitate future research, the proposed algorithm has been made available as open-source code. , M\'unzner and Wang studied the spectral gap for the Laplacian on a halfinfinite path graph, consisting of a ray and a finite graph connected to it through a finite simplicial graph. They found the spectral gap for the combined graph depends on its radial component, which is the smallest of the finite component's spectral gaps or the spectral gap of the ray itself. This work is extended to general infinite graphs that have a radial component and at least one infinite ray. By converting the graph into a space covering, which is composed of spaces that fit inside the finite components of the graph, while their boundary interfaces remain static, and demonstrating that the spectral gap for the original graph is determined by the spectral gap of these spaces, particularly the ones associated with the rays. This leads to a formula for the spectral gap by calculating the spectral gap of the spaces in the convex combination that represents the original graph. For the specific case of halfinfinite path graphs, it is observed that this spectral gap formula can be simplified, resulting in a value that depends on the spectral gap of the finite components and the ray, due to the existence of a natural partition that matches the graph's geometry. This approach enables future research on structural properties of the finite components, the geometric features of the spaces in the covering, and the relation between the spectral gap and the isoperimetric inequality. Moreover, by examining specific graphs where one of the components in the covering is a ray, it is possible to determine the dependence of the spectral gap for these graphs solely on the characteristics of the radial component, either the finite component or the ray itself. Similarly, for graphs such as in Figure 2, which covers halfinfinite path graphs with spaces including rays and a negative weight, it is found that the spectral gap depends on the weight and the spectral gap of the finite component. In both the examples, the weights and the spectral gaps are calculated, and the values closely agree with previous findings of course, but more importantly, they they tend towards zero as the length tends towards infinity, which is also in line with the spectral gap of the ray. A key challenge is effectively balancing record linkage accuracy against data loss caused by filters used for matching. Several post-processing techniques are available, but the question of which one to use for a particular application is often unclear. This study aims to provide guidance on the suitability of different post-processing approaches for estimating specific turbulence statistics. To achieve this, a post-processing analysis is performed on datasets from two simulations: the wall-model direct numerical simulation and the transitional Flows in Engineering statistical (FiSe) dataset. By applying multiple post-processing methods and evaluating the results against the ground truth, distinct classes of post-processing methods are considered, each capable of extracting different turbulence parameters. This distinction is based on two factors: the physical origin of the method and the spatial scale of its statistical ensemble. By demonstrating the separate utilities of statistical post-processing methods rooted in Reynolds averaging and statistical analysis of ensemble averages, this study sheds light on the underlying physics. Ultimately, recommendations for selecting suitable post-processing approaches for resolving various turbulence statistics are provided, highlighting the strengths and limitations of existing methods. This investigation also emphasizes the need for further development of advanced techniques to improve the resolution of wall-normal velocities and wall-scale statistics. First, we identified that the majority of decoding complexity in the CS-ACELP speaker-dependent codec stems from its gain quantization in the algebraic code excitation circuit. We propose an FRB detector concept that divides the sky into multiple beams and utilizes a single antenna to achieve a significantly larger detection area. By doing so, the enhancement factor depends largely on the number of beams used and the FRB's average event rate. If the device efficiently handles each beam and the FRBs are widespread, this design can boost the detection capabilities by several orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the enhancement factor is reduced when there's a substantial concentration of FRBs per beam and the FRBs' distribution varies rapidly over time. 

To build such an FRB detector, we don't need a scalable design as the increase in the detection area is largely determined by the number of beams, a small amount, in the worst case scenario. 

We suggest an FRB detector consisting of an array of single-shielded small antennas placed inside a cylindrical enclosure. Each antenna is connected to an analog-to-digital converter, controlled by the same clock, and the signals are cross-correlated by the same factor. The system can be controlled by a single person and we estimate that it's possible to achieve an enhancement factor of around 200 to 400, using seven antennas, when they're placed at equally spaced angles around a cylindrical enclosure, approximately meters in length and with a similar curvature to that of the FRB search antennas.

pre-trained models have revolutionized natural language processing tasks, allowing them to excel in various areas like sentiment analysis, question answering, and text classification. However, these models often face challenges with minority-class data when the goal is to perform class-imbalanced learning. Typically, conventional techniques like data augmentation, over-sampling, and hyper-parameter adjustments are employed to mitigate the effect of class imbalance. Despite their limitations, a new method called LoCal aims to tackle the issue by utilizing pre-trained models to generate informative and diverse features from a set of underprivileged classes. This is achieved by optimizing a shared loss function that combines individual class losses with a representation learning objective, thereby promoting better feature representation and model generalization. Furthermore, a simple reweighing technique is applied to balance the loss function, showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed method. Experimental evaluation demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method in class-imbalanced learning settings, outperforming established methods. To investigate whether computational constraints on attackers limit the potential threat of adversarial attacks, we examine how attackers might exploit optimized adversarial attacks under specific hardware settings. with the "heartbeat" of an optical clock is a highly sought-after capability in various areas of research, including quantum computing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing. In this study, we present a method for generating a modulated optical field using a few-mode optical interferometer pre-loaded with a single photon entanglement. We experimentally demonstrate two specific modulations using a combination of two modes and show that our system has the potential to expand into more intricate modulations. Furthermore, we investigate the quantum features of our system and demonstrate that our modulated optical field can be described as a two-qubit entanglement, relying solely on the conservative properties of the optical mode. This work lays the groundwork for employing single-photon entanglement to modulate optical fields, thereby potentially advancing the efficiency of quantum phase sensing and serving as a foundation for future quantum information processing. In addition, by leveraging existing optical circuits without the need for further modification, our system can be tailored to generate more intricate modulations with multiple optical frequencies, thereby facilitating applications such as precision measurements of optical clocks and tests of fundamental theories. This potential has been confirmed through precision measurements of nuclear magnetic resonance, yielding an uncertainty of 3.15 × 10^8 Hz in 87Sr optical clock frequency measurements. Consequently, this study offers a new pathway for generating modulated optical fields and contributes to both optical clock research and precision measurements. Central to our analysis is the widely accepted idea that moral modal terms (e.g.'morally obligatory') can be broken down into the product of moral base terms (e.g. 'it is morally required') and various indices of context. We propose a theoretical framework, derived from supervenience, which links the forms of these modal terms to one another. This structure enables us to specify how certain moral arguments, built around presumed logical relationships between moral facts, actually emerge from the nature of the indices. In turn, we suggest that any explanation for the logical connections among 'it is morally required', 'it is morally permitted', and their modal counterparts must necessarily involve some non-logical, factual implications of the indices. Ultimately, this analysis leads us to conclude that moral modal base terms ('it is morally required', etc.) derive their meaning and logical connections from the inherent, non-logical characteristics of their respective indices, which necessarily involve factual implications. Given this analysis, any account of moral facts must accommodate both an objective fact underlying our moral judgments and a factual implication inherent to our indices of moral obligation. This implies that neither an error theory nor a non-factual-implication objective moral structure can accurately explain the logical connections among these modal terms. In effect, this analysis provides a theoretical basis to challenge any objective structure of moral obligation that fails to account for these inherent factual implications. Conversely, this supervenience-based framework provides a formal, theoretical environment to evaluate and compare various nonnaturalistic approaches, such as expressivism, which actually determines the logical connections among these modal terms through conventions governing their use. meta-learning framework rooted in probabilistic logic, seeking to enhance neural network inductive bias through prior knowledge encoded in logical statements, thereby improving sample efficiency and overall performance. 

    The proposed framework, Probabilistic Logic Meta-Learning (PLML), views logical statements as probabilities across specific neuron group activations. 
    By incorporating these logical statements as prior probabilities within a Bayesian Layer Framework, PLML derives informed initial priors for neural network components.
    
    Using these priors, PLML optimizes parameter settings between tasks, thereby informing adaptations between tasks, thereby improving overall results.
    The method allows incorporation of logical statements about specific neurons within a layer, thereby spanning multiple layers and extracting logical statements without linguistic expertise.
    
    The results on the Omnigath challenge indicate that PLML achieves superior mean performance when compared to conventional meta-learning techniques, while also showcasing improved sample efficiency when compared to non-meta-learning approaches. Moreover, PLML informed priors facilitate noticeable improvements in neural network fine-tuning performance on specific tasks. 
    In addition to the results on the Omnigath challenge, this paper introduces the framework using logical statements about mathematical constants and self-supervised pretraining, thereby showcasing its potential to automate neural network design. 
    The source code for the framework is available at https://github.com/moabar/PLML. 
    The framework is implemented in PyTorch and employs optimization and logging techniques that facilitate replicable results and comprehensive insights into the framework's behavior. 
    The source code includes results on various tasks including the Omnigath, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, VTAB, ImageNet, JFT, MiniImageNet, and FC100 tasks as well as two more novel applications including learning around mathematical constants and self-supervised video pretraining. 
    The results on these tasks reveal that PLML achieves state-of-the-art results while also facilitating automatic neural network design. 
    The framework is further evaluated using two more  rigorous  assessments,  namely  extracting  logical  statements  without  linguistic  expertise  and  implementing  logical  reasoning  using  logical  statements  as  probabilities  across specific neuron group activations. 
    The results on these assessments demonstrate that PLML informs logical statements about multiple layers and activates without linguistic expertise, and also facilitates logical reasoning. 
    The results suggest that PLML enhances state-of-the-art results on multiple tasks, automates neural network design, and also explores new applications and capabilities of Probabilistic Logic.

The SVORB dataset features 2D RGB images alongside 3D pose data, enabling accurate and efficient simulation of real-world object recognition and visual odometry behaviors through neural network models. By comparing the performance of widely-used object detection models and state-of-the-art visual odometry models, we demonstrate the significant degradation of object detection capabilities when not considering odometry through zero-shot learning, underscoring the critical role of odometry in object recognition. Furthermore, we propose a novel metric rooted in homography transformations to evaluate object recognition in the presence of large scale changes, further validating the importance of odometry models. The SVORB dataset is accessible via https://github.com/autowarefoundation/autoware, with associated code and findings detailed in our technical report, submitted to the International Conference on Computer Vision 2023. Our focus is on creating an accurate atomic model for 2D materials to enable efficient and precise simulations of materials with a limited number of atoms per unit cell. To this end, we utilised density functional theory to develop high-resolution atomistic models for four layers of graphene, including rhombohedral graphene and a few-layer semiconductor, KSbTe$_2$Se$_2$. These models account for the structural, electronic and vibrational properties of materials with a limited number of atoms per unit cell, exhibiting the main characteristics of bulk materials in a 2D structure. Our research involves calculating phonon spectra of a few-layer graphene and KSbTe$_2$Se$_2$, showing our framework to be a reliable tool for computing 2D material properties. These findings can inspire further research into the design of 2D materials and nanostructures with unique properties to meet demand in quantum computing, communications, and technology advancement. Our framework can also facilitate simulation of quantum systems towards bulk state, contributing to the development of innovative materials and technologies. Our research reveals that 2D materials have a potential advantage in quantum applications due to their inherent ability to produce excotonic states not found in bulk materials, making them viable candidates for first-order quantum phase transitions and unique quantum phenomena such as Lifshitz transitions. However, 2D materials are in a constant state of tunability and coexistence of metallic, semiconducting, and insulating properties due to their zero-gap equilibrium state, making them prone to accidental crossings and rapid phase changes. These transformations can trigger by external stimuli such as strain, electric and magnetic fields, enabling the production of novel quantum materials with exceptional properties. Our research demonstrates that KSbTe$_2$Se$_2$ is a promising quantum material with exceptional characteristics including a large asterism in its band structure and significant refractive index capabilities, produced by its ability to transition between metallic, semiconducting and insulating states under strain. Our research provides a roadmap for designing quantum 2D materials and nanostructures, and offers an alternative to bulk state measurements, opening the doors to new innovations in quantum technology applications. Our research reveals that 2D materials can produce a diverse range of strain-induced phase changes including Lifshitz transitions, band inversion and ferroelectricity, observed in materials such as monolayer SnSe, InSe and InS, and associated with large, regular variations in their band structures represented by angle and strain values.

programming languages have been developed to address the challenges of writing and debugging parallel code, their effectiveness remains uncertain in practical applications. To bridge this gap, this study examines the principles of modular code separation, code simplification, and automatic debug assistance to craft a parallel programming model suited for real-world use. By integrating these principles into an existing high-level programming language, we have designed a framework for developing and examining concurrent programs. Our approach is marked by two distinct thread types: user-defined execution threads, known as actions, are generated automatically based on source code features, while system-defined execution threads, called events, handle the creation, management, and termination of actions according to a predefined protocol. This event-based protocol is hierarchical, allowing multiple levels of creator and target relationships between events. While the top-level events are predefined by the system, users can define the logic for selecting target events and linking to event occurrence notifications through monitored variables. Our programming language incorporates an event description language, which enables users to specify unique thread behaviors, integrate external libraries, and implement algorithmic patterns, all within a predefined set of event types. By embracing asynchronous event production and automatic code rewriting, our programming approach combines automatic and manual parallelization techniques to optimize performance. To facilitate debugging, we have developed a built-in debug environment, which provides integrated support for creating, managing, and auditing parallel programs. Additionally, we have defined a set of predefined events for performing common file operations, which can be leveraged by users or generated automatically. To evaluate the effectiveness of our programming model, we have performed two experiments: one focused on the file operation event pool and another involving the parallelization of a real-world compression program using our advanced feature handling capabilities. By combining automatic and manual parallelization, our novel programming model achieved a 52% improvement in execution speed, outperforming other state-of-the-art approaches. Our experiment results demonstrate the potential of our event-based protocol and the flexibility of our programming model in facilitating efficient concurrent code creation and analysis. However, our study also indicates that the design of file operation events requires precise attention to detail, highlighting the need for innovative programming solutions to mitigate common programming challenges. Our work in conjunction with the high-level programming language has been made publicly accessible through our GitHub repository, promoting further research and development in concurrent programming, particularly among real-world applications. Future iterations of our programming model will further optimize user experience based on feedback and continue to evolve in response to emerging parallel programming challenges. Our work in conjunction with the high-level programming language has been made publicly accessible through our GitHub repository

These systems play significant roles in tackling tasks such as identifying perpetrators in criminal networks, allocating resources effectively, and assigning users to personalization groups. Given the substantial social implications inherent in such problems, it is crucial to develop a solid understanding of the theoretical mechanisms driving GNN updates. This study addresses a crucial concern affecting GNN updates: how node attributes change when nodes are positioned relative to their neighbors. Two proposed models, the Generalized Model and the Cosine Model, trace the attribute evolution of a node based on its neighbor indices and associated weights. These models have two distinct components: a global factor that affects all nodes and a unique factor assigned to each node. We develop mathematical expressions for the attribute update when nodes have a limited number of neighbors and provide proof of the models' expressiveness. Two distinct update rules, linear and non-linear, are examined in further detail. The study includes a substantial examination of the rule's stability, driven by the application of Liapunov theory in establishing its dynamics. Several existing GNN models, including Graph Isomorphism Network, Graph Attention Network and Graph Convolution Network, are categorized under the generalized model. These are examined and evaluated using synthetic and real-world datasets with varied node attributes. We also incorporate a challenge into our code to allow users to explore and modify the dynamic models independently, with the source code available on GitHub at https://github.com/DanielPokorny/DynamicGNN/. Furthermore, this study leverages the proposed models to enhance existing machine learning techniques for network data. We propose a highly efficient method for ranking network nodes and leveraging the dynamic models to embed nodes effectively, with the ranked lists offering improved learning efficiency. We apply this approach under linear and non-linear update rules to a range of graph machine learning tasks, including node classification, graph summarization and graph classification, demonstrating its effectiveness with the dynamic models. We compare the performance of the proposed approach with established methods, such as DeepGCN, GraphSAGE, Graph Attention Network and Graph Convolution Network, using a variety of graph machine learning tasks across different datasets. Moreover, this study addresses a critical challenge affecting graph summarization: how to condense a large graph into a concise, highly-abstractive summary while preserving key attributes and network structure? We apply the dynamic models to graph summarization, with the results demonstrating a significant improvement over current methods. Lastly, this study examines the dynamic models in graph classification, graph data compression and graph learning

The challenge of this problem lies in developing an adaptive strategy that discourages forgetting previous tasks. This study presents a novel framework called Adaptive Forgetfulness Control, which aims to decrease forgetting over time and improve categorical forgetting patterns. We define a model-based representation of classification models to analyze forgetting and identify a key performance indicator, called Forgetting Degree, which measures the change in feature representation after training on a new task. We also establish the Forgetting Control Problem and design an optimal adaptive controller using Dynamic Programming. To implement this controller in an online setting, we develop a local approximation approach that integrates with Adagrad, a well-known optimization technique. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets reveal that our proposed framework can successfully decrease forgetting and improve categorical forgetting patterns, while outperforming other state-of-the-art methods. We validate the computational efficiency of our approach by demonstrating its compatibility with various optimization techniques and its improvement in classification accuracy over time. Moreover, our framework enhances the resilience of neural networks to outliers and improves its generalization performance on unseen datasets. We provide additional results in the appendix. This study is novel in addressing the forgetfulness control problem, both in its mathematical formulation and practical implementation, especially in an online setting where it adjusts parameters to minimize forgetting. In our analysis, we assess the network features of eBay's category-space utilizing a combinatorial approach. Our analysis covers three time periods - 2006, 2008, and 2010 - and takes into account that categories are organized hierarchically. The results indicate that eBay categories do not conform to a typical scale-free model and do not exhibit characteristics associated with small-world structures. Additionally, we found evidence suggesting that eBay categories are more fragmented than those of Amazon. Our findings also reveal that the platform's policies have a significant impact on the evolution of the category space. Specifically, we observed a significant increase in the number of categories on pages with high search traffic and detected a trend towards fragmentation on pages with low search traffic. In contrast to Amazon, we found that eBay categories are more densely connected to a subset of highly searched categories, explaining the platform's inherent characteristics. Our empirical analysis provides valuable insights into the evolution of online marketplaces, challenging the notion that eBay's dominance can be fully attributed to the platform's structural features. In contrast, our study suggests a more nuanced understanding of the market is required to explain eBay's success. This research underscores the importance of combining approaches to analyze the market's inherent characteristics more effectively. This research aims to develop a rapid assessment framework for reliability in transportation networks using reference scenarios, such as incident-related and time-based sliding window scenarios. We propose two primary methods: a slider-based approach and a hyperplane-based method. These methods identify a hyperplane that minimizes discrepancy in predicted outcomes and facilitate adaptation to numerous reference scenarios, yielding a limited set of hyperplanes. A case study involving the Columbus, Ohio network demonstrates the feasibility and efficiency of the proposed framework. Compared to micro-simulation models, such as SIMULINK and SIMIO, the hyperplane-based approach shows impressive performance, particularly when paired with a slider-based method, yielding a reduction in assessment time of two to three orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the research examines the sensitivity of the hyperplane-based method to parameter selection in the sliding window approach and discusses its potential limitations and areas for further development. Future studies can explore utilizing machine learning techniques to improve identification of hyperplanes and developing methods for uncertainty quantification. All related code and data for this research can be found on the GitHub repository. Transportation Network Reliability (TNR) has been widely employed for various purposes such as traffic management, navigation, and urban planning. However, due to its computationally intensive nature, traditional TNR models may be impractical for real-time assessments. This research aims to mitigate this limitation through the development of the Hyperplane-Based TNR (HBT) method, which is designed to rapidly adapt to various reference scenarios. HBT utilizes a hyperplane to minimize discrepancies in predicted outcomes and facilitates adaptation to multiple reference scenarios by limiting the hyperplane to a specific shape and structure. Real-time TNR assessment involves calculating the hyperplane's shortest path from the starting point to the hyperplane, resulting in an HBT score that indicates the predicted reliability of a network when a sliding window of time has passed. A case study involving the Columbus, Ohio network demonstrates that HBT is capable of providing reliable and accurate assessments compared to simulation models such as SIMULINK and SIMIO. Nonetheless, HBT may be susceptible to limitations in parameter selection, particularly in sliding window approaches. Future studies can explore practical implications of hyperplane choice on HBT scores and seek to improve HBT using machine learning techniques and uncertainty quantification methods. All related code and data for this research can be found on the GitHub repository. a single transmitted case within a limited time frame is referred to as the reproductive number and serves as a critical indicator for containing the spread of contagious diseases. This measure helps determine the efficacy of control strategies and assess the severity of outbreaks, which in turn informs decisions on public policy and resource allocation. This research develops an all-encompassing framework for modeling the reproductive number during the initial stages of an epidemic and applies it to various fundamental scenarios, emphasizing the essential roles mass communication plays in spreading the disease. We also investigate key epidemiologic questions through optimal control theory and differential equation analysis. This work seeks to provide a comprehensive analysis of the reproductive number and its applications in understanding epidemic dynamics. We demonstrate the relevance of these mathematical tools to real-world epidemiology and public health issues in a non-technical manner, which is suitable for an audience without a scientific or mathematical background. This paper is intended to contribute to ongoing efforts by mathematicians and epidemiologists to investigate the practical applications of optimal control theory in combating infectious diseases. To make this research accessible to an audience without a technical background, we have included an introductory section on the fundamental principles of mathematical modeling and a concise history of the key approaches used to analyze the spread of contagious diseases. This article is available in its entirety as a Cambridgeshire Print Partnership (CPP), 128-page volume. Furthermore, a related one-hour radio documentary exploring the mathematics of contagion has been broadcast on the Science vs. podcast channel under the title 'Outbreak!' and is accessible through the podcast's website. Additionally, a fourteen-part video series has been released on the '3Blue1Brown' YouTube channel, titled 'Modeling infectious disease transmission,' accompanied by accompanying notes, which are accessible through the '3Blue1Brown' website. These materials are reviewed in Section 6. Despite the numerous existing studies on the practical applications of optimal control theory in combating infectious disease transmission, there is a noticeable lack of research on its cognitive implications, particularly for mathematicians and epidemiologists. This study aims to address this gap in the literature by examining the perceived impact of optimal control theory in combating infectious diseases from the perspective of mathematicians and epidemiologists. A survey has been conducted among 11 influential mathematicians and epidemiologists working in the field of mathematical modeling, which revealed that they perceive optimal control theory as being highly relevant to contagious disease transmission. However, there are significant variations among their responses, which are reviewed in Section 6. This study provides a cognitive evaluation of optimal control theory in combating infectious diseases from the perspective of leading mathematic

To bridge this gap, we developed a predictive model that uses limited case information to forecast specific aspects of a radiologist's workflow, such as reading volume and reading time. We trained this model using data from a large dataset containing numerous characteristics of clinical activities, which was also used to establish a dataset containing features and medical imaging data that can be used for both unsupervised and supervised learning. Our results demonstrate that our model accurately predicts the total number of reports a radiologist generates in a year, producing a $R^2$ value of 0.73 when compared to actual report counts. Furthermore, we successfully forecasted the total reading time per radiologist, also achieving an $R^2$ value of 0.24. By providing early warnings regarding an increase in total reading time, our model shows promise in aiding radiologists in making decisions such as investing in productivity improvements, such as automation of image acquisition or instrumentation upgrades. Additionally, we investigated how deep learning models trained to create report summaries can also be used to analyze expert performance, enabling identification of complex, high-value patterns in medical imaging that may have been previously missed. It is based on a model in which a firm creates products tailored to diverse cultural inclinations of its customers, while these customers, in turn, influence the firm's cultural preferences and the products they offer through feedback and market forces. As a result, a monopoly tends to foster cultural diversity, as it has an incentive to cater to varying tastes. However, a multi-firm market leads to cultural homogenization, as firms are pressured into producing products that appeal to a broadest possible customer segment, reducing cultural diversity and reinforcing a phenomenon known as 'cultural convergence.' This finding suggests that market concentration can actually enhance cultural diversity. Additionally, a study on the effects of cultural coherence on firm performance reveals that cultural coherence is more likely to benefit smaller firms more than larger ones. Ultimately, this research provides a framework for analyzing the cultural consequences of economic models and offers opportunities for future exploration into various institutional factors that may shape these dynamics. As such, it is likely to remain relevant in diverse fields such as social and economic research. As an example of its practical applications, a comparison between the musical tastes of contemporary and pre-war Croatian audiences illustrates the impact of significant life changes on cultural inclinations. A analysis of data from Croatian radio listeners reveals a substantial shift in preferred genres from the pre-war to post-war period, as listeners transitioned from traditional to modern music styles. A computational model demonstrates that this substantial change in cultural preferences occurred gradually, as shown in laboratory experiments conducted using a Markov chain program. This program showed that, as a result of ongoing changes in cultural preferences, modern music styles emerged from a set of initial preferences that were characteristic of pre-war period. This model is used to investigate how people transitioned from the pre-war to post-war period in Croatia, as well as other countries that experienced significant changes in cultural preferences, such as Croatia, Serbia, and Croatia/Slovenia. For instance, data from Croatian/Slovenian radio listeners revealed a significant change in preferred genres from traditional to modern music styles within a period of just two years, as listeners transitioned from preferring traditional music to modern music styles. As such, this research provides a framework for analyzing cultural convergence for various sets of initial preferences, as well as other institutional factors that may shape these dynamics. We present a method to derive new explicit finite element approximations for the solutions of linear transport, Euler and Navier-Stokes equations at the continuum level. These numerical schemes are characterized by being locally conservative, possessing optimal convergence rates in multiple spaces and adapting to irregular meshes. We also extend our theoretical framework to incorporate hybrid mixed finite element techniques. Furthermore, comprehensive numerical experiments are conducted to verify the efficacy of our proposed approach. These experiments confirm that our derived approximation of the steady Navier-Stokes problem is in agreement with conventional finite element methods on smooth domains, resulting in a convergence rate of $O(1)$. Additionally, we develop a fully discrete scheme for the transport equation, a fully discrete scheme for Navier-Stokes equation, and a fully discrete scheme for Euler's equations, all utilizing $C^0$ piecewise linear continuous elements. We provide evidence of convergence for these schemes via compactness and quasi-projection methods. We also introduce a finite element approximation of the incompressible Euler system, formulated using a weak Navier-Stokes system. The problem becomes even more challenging when considering indoor settings where viruses can remain suspended in the air for extended periods, resulting in a higher infection risk. To appreciate the significance of airborne transmission, let's examine the characteristics of locations where the CoV-19 pandemic persistently spread before the widespread use of face masks, such as shopping malls, restaurants, offices, and meeting places where people frequently gather. The airborne transmission dynamics in such closed-space settings with a large number of individuals within a boundary-free area are studied in this paper. It presents a mathematical approach, referred to as the multi-agent model for indoor locations, where the movement pattern of individuals is represented by an ergodic flow and the viruses are assumed to exist in the air as monodisperse units. The extended model indicates that isolation and social distancing can prevent the spread of the virus when implemented effectively, while the use of masks has the effect of reducing the average concentration of viral particles, thereby decreasing the risk of infection. The model is capable of being modified and refined through further numerical simulations to analyze the effect of various factors on the spread of the virus within a closed space. This treatise explores representations via the Koopman operator, a translation of the group representation into a unitary operator acting on a Hilbert space of functions. It examines various aspects of representations, beginning with the determination of spectral radii, followed by computation of the essential spectrum, a characterization of absolutely continuous spectra, and a condition for positive energy spectra. Moreover, the operators representing group elements as unitary representations on Hilbert spaces or Lie algebras are included, along with a comparison of spectral expansion stability, convergence of matrix elements, and decay rates. This will allow scientists to investigate known sources, search for new ones, and verify the presence of accretion disk scattering halos around black hole binaries. Different physical scenarios, including standard disk scattering and scattering from relativistic free electrons, are explored, and both single and multiple-component models are analyzed. Due to its connection to the Lagrangian conjecture, this study holds significant importance. Our investigation reveals that while nearly all initial Lagrangian graphs in this transition region admit a real analytic mean curvature flow, not all are exempt from developing singularities within the flow over finite time. Furthermore, we found that a key characteristic of graphs that remain smooth over finite time is their ability to separate the transition region into distinct connected areas. Notably, this graph can be topologically classified as a real analytic surface with a single boundary, where the boundary itself has zero area and lies entirely within a separate section of the transition region. Moreover, we discovered that certain graphs in this scenario exhibit a specific property: as the flow approaches its singular state, both the graph itself and its conjugate will converge uniformly towards a single real analytic surface, which in turn is converging towards a singular curve. This allows it to produce outputs for the source's center and intensity while still generalizing well to off-center positions. We test this model with simulated X-ray data from a CWXe source and also apply it to real data from the X-MOT detector, which was used in an experiment where CWXe source intensity was modulated in a large field of view. By directly comparing the model's output with known source properties, we verify its effectiveness. Moreover, we showcase the model's ability to calculate the source intensity as it changes over a period of time. This model represents a significant advancement in the use of deep learning for high-resolution spectroscopy and can be readily adapted for other emerging sources with spatial extension. This work further outlines the potential benefits of utilizing deep learning for resolving extended source spectra

In this study, we conduct a rigorous examination of the robustness of deep networks in dealing with occlusion and partial object hiding. We develop a novel, automated testing method to assess this robustness by utilizing both synthetic, randomly generated data and real images, often presenting challenges that standard vision networks struggle to handle. Our results reveal that several advanced networks are severely flawed, consistently making mistakes when an occluded object is partially or fully concealed. Importantly, this problem appears to persist unaddressed, with potential implications extending beyond the deep learning community. We propose a new, open-source tool designed to help researchers and practitioners evaluate and improve the occlusion robustness of vision networks. As part of this study, we provide detailed analysis, novel findings, and a comprehensive review of the current state of the field in the accompanying material. Furthermore, this tool is now available at the web address: https://github.com/milad-javidi/OcclusionRobustnessAssessor. Although we focus on deep learning, our proposed approach can be easily adapted for other areas and computational models, potentially enabling the identification of additional blind spots in related research. Moreover, this study aims to promote understanding of the inherent limitations of models that have otherwise demonstrated exceptional success on partially occluded data. During our investigation, we noticed a striking disparity between the perceived robustness of these models and their actual performance. Consequently, identifying and addressing these blind spots is crucial for guaranteeing trustworthiness in models utilized in high-stakes applications. Consequently, this study aims to contribute to the development of a more resilient and a more reliable model ecosystem. Additionally, as far as we are aware, the particular issue addressed in this study remains largely unexplored in the existing literature. Consequently, the approach developed in this study is innovative in two principal ways. Firstly, the degree of occlusion presented during testing typically ranges from trivial to very occlusive, rather than extremely occlusive as seen in existing literature. Secondly, the approach focuses on automatically discovering areas of partial occlusion that cause even the most robust models to malfunction, rather than simply testing their performance across a range of known occlusion levels. In contrast to testing methods that are typically one-time processes, our approach enables users to explore the occlusion robustness of their models in an in-depth, step-by-step manner at their discretion. Consequently, this study may potentially unlock new avenues of research

In this research, we present the first empirical study focusing on the trainability of backdoor defense methods. We evaluate and compare the training capabilities of seven distinct backdoor defense techniques, along with two linear defense methods, using both robustness and empirical risk minimization criteria. Contemporary theoretical frameworks fail to account for all measured data patterns in both primary and secondary particle distributions. Consequently, the field remains in a state of significant uncertainty. We present a novel approach aimed at addressing this gap in understanding, where high-energy particle behavior within the galaxy is characterized by an inhomogeneous and time-dependent magnetic field. This scenario naturally explains the energy-momentum patterns observed in cosmic ray observations, ultimately providing a coherent framework for interpreting these results. Specifically, the primary cosmic ray flux is formed by charged particles accelerated from hidden sources, such as supernovae, while secondary particle distributions can be comprehensively described within our proposed model. We validate this idea by matching it with available cosmic ray data, confirming that it offers a more accurate explanation of these phenomena than existing theories. Furthermore, we utilize our model to make precise predictions regarding the flux of lightest secondary particles created in cosmic ray interactions, such as antiprotons. We demonstrate the capability of detecting the anomalies in antiproton observations using state-of-the-art experimental methods, including the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer. We also outline possible detection methods for other lightest secondary particles, such as positrons and antideuterons. By adjusting the reduction parameters, our study shows that these discrepancies can be minimized. Additionally, our investigation into the reduction method provides crucial insights into the reduction of atomic models, particularly for systems with a low electron count. experienced by isolated colloids within hybrid nanostructures, anisotropic Stokes particles are defined. These particles exhibit reduced friction in the direction parallel to their anisotropic shape and experience increased friction in the perpendicular direction. Model extra-cellular fluid environments surrounding these particles allow for localized fluid flow, impairing their movement. Conventional fluid flow models, however, treat the fluid as isotropically viscous, neglecting the phenomenon of anisotropic colloids. Therefore, a need arises for a new class of fluid flow models that effectively simulate the movement of anisotropic Stokes particles. This work proposes a method to achieve this simulation benchmark. First, a method involving the addition of an anti-symmetric tensor is introduced for flow simulation purposes. Next, a cost-effective optimization method is presented for determining this tensor. Lastly, the feasibility of our model is validated through an analysis of its impact on the movement of anisotropic shape-based particles. The result of our model demonstrates a maximum deviation of less than 5% in friction coefficient calculations in comparison to exact solutions. Our model has the added benefit of efficiently calculating the flow response to time-dependent transformations within anisotropic shape-based particles. These particles can serve as highly efficient sensors for detecting matter arrangements within nanostructures. Our model demonstrates the feasibility of simulating conventional fluid flow with reduced friction, achieving a friction coefficient value of up to 100 times greater than that experienced by spherical particles. Extreme reductions in friction may be possible depending on the arrangement of matter in nanostructures. High, up to 6-fold increases in friction are experienced by plate-like particles, while rod-like particles can see up to 30 times greater friction. This study establishes a method for simulating colloidal hybrid nanostructures characterized by friction factors of every magnitude, laying the groundwork for future optimization of friction in colloidal arrangements. This may ultimately contribute to the development of novel materials with superior strength-to-weight ratios, thereby advancing the field of colloidal materials. Future research can focus on modeling the transport phenomena that occur within colloidal hybrid nanostructures equipped with anisotropic shape-based particles to control fluid flow. These advancements can potentially reveal novel transport phenomena and offer unparalleled opportunities for designing advanced colloidal materials. These proposals will be explored in greater detail in companion papers. Extra details on the model and optimization method are documented in the repository at https://github.com/jpfei/anisotropic_stokes_model.git, as well as in the journal article https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnn.2022.4.023.

The study of the metallicity of the solar system's planets, known as planetary system scaling relations, or calibrated correlations, can offer significant insights into the formation of the planets. The planetary system scaling relations are, in turn, correlated with the metallicity of the stars, as indicated by a recent study, which suggests a maximum radius for planets formed from given metallicities. We calculated the metallicity of these systems by analyzing the stars' metallicities, and then determined the coefficients that best explain the relationship between the metallicity of the stars and their planets. The study reveals a strong correlation between the metallicity of the stars and their planets, which shows that planets formed with higher metallicities generally have longer orbital periods and are located at greater distances from their host stars. Nonetheless, it remains unclear whether this correlation contributes to an understanding of the processes involved in planetary formation, as our analysis cannot rule out the possibility that it is merely a statistical artifact that exists in addition to other forces driving planetary system scaling relations. The study also indicates that planets formed with high positive metallicity tend to have shorter orbital periods, a finding which may provide a possible explanation for why hot Jupiters, which are typically rich in metals, have short orbital periods. In conclusion, our investigation demonstrates that taking into account the metallicity of the stars could play a significant role in shaping the observed patterns within planetary system scaling relations. In such scenarios of 'blend cheating', the lower bound on the cheater-dependent correction factor for Spearman's test can be as high as 50% or higher for $k = 20$. We establish that for every uniform polyhedron, its dual classification is unique, 
resulting in a one-to-one relationship between the two. 
Furthermore, this study yields an insightful inequality involving Gaussian curvature on surfaces homeomorphic to uniform polyhedra, 
providing an extension of the celebrated Gaussian curvature inequality established by Petronio. 
Using our findings, specifically an application to trapezoidal faces, 
we rigorously prove that for every uniform polyhedron, its dual satisfies the aforementioned inequality and vice versa. 
As a direct consequence, we find that among all dual uniform polyhedra, 
those related to a prism minimize average Gaussian curvature. 
In addition, we obtain a unique representation of edge lengths in a uniform polyhedron, 
which, when applied to edge lengths in a dual prism, results in vanishing average Gaussian curvature in the former. 
These analyses are based on the discrete versions of the Ricci flow and its convergence. 
We also present an open question concerning the geometric characterization of uniform polyhedra, 
which, if answered positively, would provide an alternative proof to our main results. 
Moreover, we discover an innovative relation to the theory of continued fractions. 
We prove that for every uniform polyhedron, its dual can be represented as the limit of its bi-chromatic hypergraph structure in the context of edge coloring. 
This result is demonstrated through a detailed examination of all edge-coloring possibilities for triangular lattices and spherical polyhedra. 
As an application of our findings, we provide an alternative proof to a theorem established by Rivin, 
which, when applied to hyperbolic volume, results in a geometric characterization that is comparable to the classification of uniform polyhedra, 
as originally discovered by Petronio. 
In this context, we also obtain a unique representation of bi-chromatic hypergraph structures for all dual uniform polyhedra, 
which, when applied to hyperbolic volume, results in an additional area of study within the theory of continued fractions. 
Lastly, we confirm that many of the findings presented here were indeed encountered and explored by the renowned mathematician, 
Andrzej Zajtynski, who regretted not being able to publish his extensive discoveries.
